definition: Artificial intelligence in eLearning refers to the application of computational systems and machine learning techniques to support, enhance, and automate processes within digital education ecosystems.
details: The eLearning ecosystem is composed of multiple interconnected layers that collectively support the creation, distribution, management, delivery, governance, and optimization of digital learning experiences. These include learning content creation systems, authoring tools, learning management systems, course marketplaces, public education infrastructures, learner analytics systems, assessment mechanisms, adaptive learning technologies, tutoring systems, and governance frameworks.

explainer.lead: Artificial intelligence in eLearning uses computational and machine-learning techniques to improve digital education. It can help create content, tailor learning activities, assess progress, and automate parts of course delivery and management.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a learning app as a coach who watches which questions you find easy or difficult. It can then suggest what to practise next, while also helping teachers organise lessons and see how learners are doing. The aim is to make digital learning more responsive rather than giving everyone exactly the same path.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, AI components can sit inside authoring tools, learning management systems, tutoring systems, assessment services, and learner-analytics platforms. They use learning content and activity or assessment data to produce outputs such as recommendations, feedback, adaptive pathways, or operational insights. Implementations should check that these outputs remain educationally sound and that automation does not bypass appropriate governance.
tiers.paperLevel: Let D denote learning content, learner activity, and assessment observations within a digital education ecosystem. AI in eLearning applies computational or learned functions f(D) to support decisions such as content selection, feedback, assessment, adaptation, analytics, or administration. Its scope covers the full socio-technical learning system, so evaluating a predictive output alone does not establish the quality of the resulting learning experience.

explainer.example: A learner answers several algebra questions incorrectly in an online course. An adaptive tutoring component uses those assessment results to select a simpler practice exercise and provide targeted feedback, while the learner-analytics system records the difficulty so the next activity can be adjusted.

usedIn.name: Learning management systems
usedIn.detail: Support the management and delivery of digital courses and learning experiences.

usedIn.name: Adaptive learning technologies
usedIn.detail: Adjust learning activities or pathways in response to information about the learner.

usedIn.name: Learner analytics systems
usedIn.detail: Analyse learning activity and outcomes to inform educational decisions and optimisation.

usedIn.name: Tutoring and assessment systems
usedIn.detail: Provide automated support, feedback, or evaluation within digital learning.

explainer.intuition: A conventional online course largely follows a fixed design, while an AI-supported course can use information about content, learners, and outcomes to assist decisions. The same idea also extends beyond tutoring to content creation, course administration, analytics, and governance.
howItWorks: Gather inputs from learning content, learner activity, assessments, and course-management processes.
Apply computational or machine-learning techniques to identify patterns or generate a proposed output.
Turn that output into feedback, a recommended activity, an adaptive pathway, an assessment result, or an administrative action.
Use learner responses and system outcomes to support further analytics and optimisation within the applicable governance framework.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects automation and learner-specific support across the many layers of digital education, rather than treating online learning as merely content on a website. This can help coordinate instruction, assessment, delivery, and improvement at a scale that fixed processes handle less flexibly.
misconceptions: It is not limited to chatbots or automated tutoring; it also includes content, analytics, assessment, infrastructure, and management processes.
It does not make every course automatically adaptive; adaptation is one application among many.
An AI-generated recommendation or assessment is not automatically educationally valid and still belongs within a governance framework.
